title: CVE-2026-69192 in ip-address 10.1.0 (SSRF via inconsistent IPv4 parsing)
description: The transitive package **`ip-address@10.1.0`** (pinned via `pnpm-lock.yaml`) is affected by CVE-2026-69192: `Address4` decodes IPv4 octets with a leading zero as **decimal**, whereas the WHATWG URL host parser, `inet_aton`, and `getaddrinfo` decode them as **octal**. The library and the network stack disagree about which host a string names, enabling SSRF and trust-boundary bypass when `ip-address` is used to validate destination hosts. Fixed in `10.3.1`. Published 2026-08-03; references include the upstream fix commit `beaugunderson/ip-address@56368cb` and Red Hat CVE advisory.
impact: An attacker who can influence any host/IP validation performed through this chain can craft an address (e.g. `012.0.0.1`, `0x0a.1`) that the library validates as a benign/internal host while the actual DNS/connect layer resolves it to an arbitrary target, bypassing SSRF host allow/deny checks. Scope is Changed because the parsing confusion crosses a security authority boundary between validation and resolution.
technical_analysis:
**Root cause:** `ip-address` ≤ 10.1.0 treats an IPv4 octet written with a leading zero (e.g. `012`) as base-10. The WHATWG host parser, libc `inet_aton`, and `getaddrinfo` treat it as octal.  `new Address4('012.0.0.1')` therefore returns a different address than the one the network stack will actually connect to. Any validation/allowlist built on `ip-address` can be bypassed by an attacker-controlled host string.

**Dependency chain observed in `pnpm-lock.yaml` (trivy `--list-all-pkgs` graph):**
```
@kubernetes/client-node@1.4.0(encoding@0.1.13)
  > socks-proxy-agent@8.0.5
    > socks@2.8.7
      > ip-address@10.1.0
```
Application code reaches `@kubernetes/client-node` via dynamic `import()` (lazy load) in `src/services/pipelines/udfRunner.ts:56` and `src/services/orchestration/runners/k8s-runtime.ts:61`, so the chain is loaded at runtime in k8s-enabled deployments.

**Trivy excerpt:**
```

VulnerabilityID=CVE-2026-69192  PkgName=ip-address  InstalledVersion=10.1.0  FixedVersion=10.3.1  Severity=HIGH
CVSS redhat:8.6 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N)  CWE-20 / CWE-918
PrimaryURL=https://avd.aquasec.com/nvd/cve-2026-69192
```

The direct dependency it rolls up to is `@kubernetes/client-node@1.4.0` (confirmed in `package.json`).
remediation_steps:
The fix version `ip-address@10.3.1` is a *minor* bump within the range that `socks@2.8.7` declares (`^10.0.0`), so re-resolving the lockfile will pick it up automatically. Options:
1. Bump the **direct** dependency in `package.json`: raise `@kubernetes/client-node` to a version whose closure pins `ip-address@>=10.3.1` (≥ 1.4.x patch that vendors the fix), then `pnpm install`.
2. Add a pnpm override to force the transitive resolution, then commit the updated `pnpm-lock.yaml`:
   `pnpm.overrides: { "ip-address@<10.3.1": "^10.3.1" }` in `package.json`.
3. Re-run `pnpm install` and confirm with `trivy fs pnpm-lock.yaml` that `ip-address` resolves to `>=10.3.1`.
Do not edit `pnpm-lock.yaml` by hand; use `pnpm.overrides` so the lockfile stays reproducible.

title: CVE-2026-41907 in uuid 13.0.0 (OOB write in v3/v5/v6 with caller-provided buffer)
description: The direct dependency **`uuid@13.0.0`** (pinned via `package.json` and `pnpm-lock.yaml`) is affected by CVE-2026-41907: `v3`, `v5`, and `v6` accept an external output buffer + offset but do not reject out-of-range writes (small `buf` or large `offset`), allowing silent partial writes into caller-provided memory. Fixed in `14.0.0` (also patched at `11.1.1`, `12.0.1`, `13.0.1`). References include upstream fix commits `uuidjs/uuid@32389c8` and `@3d2c5b0`.
impact: If `uuid.v5` (or v3/v6) is ever invoked with a caller-controlled output buffer and offset, the caller can coerce a write outside the intended buffer range, corrupting adjacent Node.js process memory. This is a memory-corruption primitive with integrity impact; the current application code paths do not pass the optional buf/offset arguments, so exploitation would require a future change or a dependency-chain caller.
technical_analysis:
**Root cause:** `uuid` prior to the fix does not bounds-check the optional `(buf, offset)` out-params on `v3`/`v5`/`v6`. Passing a `buf` that is too small or an `offset` larger than the buffer silently writes out of range.

**Application usage:** `uuid@^13.0.0` is a direct dependency in `package.json`. Import scan found:
- `src/config/foundryMulter.ts:4` — `v4` (not affected)
- `src/middleware/correlationId.ts:2` — `v4` (not affected)
- `src/services/branchContext.ts:22,44` — `v5` (**affected API**, but called as `uuidv5(name, DNS_NS)` with no `buf`/`offset`)
- `src/services/quiver/rids.ts:11` — `v7` (not affected)

The vulnerable `v5` symbol is used, so per the evidence ladder this is `vulnerable_symbol_used`, but the specific OOB-write invocation pattern is not present in existing code.

```

CVSS ghsa:7.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N)  CWE-787 / CWE-823
```

`uuid` is a direct dependency, so no `introduced_by` chain applies.

Because `^13.0.0` already permits `13.0.1`, a plain `pnpm update uuid` may pick the fix without editing `package.json`; committing the regenerated lockfile is sufficient. No code changes are required.

Direct `uuid` imports confirmed at src/config/foundryMulter.ts:4, src/middleware/correlationId.ts:2 (both `v4`, unaffected), src/services/quiver/rids.ts:11 (`v7`, unaffected). title: CVE-2026-13676 in fast-uri 3.1.2 via ajv (URL security-policy bypass via Unicode hostname canonicalization)
description: The transitive package **`fast-uri@3.1.2`** (pinned via `pnpm-lock.yaml` through `ajv`) is affected by CVE-2026-13676: `fast-uri` versions 2.3.1 through 3.1.2 and 4.0.0 fail to canonicalize Unicode (IDN) hostnames for HTTP-family URLs — the IDN conversion path calls a helper that does not exist on the global `URL` constructor — so `normalize()` / `equal()` return values that differ from a WHATWG-compatible URL parser. Applications using `fast-uri` (directly or via `ajv`'s URI format validation) to enforce hostname policy can be bypassed. Fixed in `3.1.3` / `4.0.1` / `2.4.2`.
impact: Hostname allow/deny decisions made on the fast-uri-normalized value can disagree with what the actual HTTP client (Node WHATWG URL) resolves, letting an attacker-registered look-alike Unicode (IDN) host pass a host-equality or origin check. This is a security-policy bypass with Integrity impact; no direct confidentiality or availability effect on its own.
technical_analysis:
**Root cause:** `fast-uri` ≤ 3.1.2 (and 4.0.0) calls a nonexistent helper for IDN/Unicode hostname conversion, silently leaving the host in Unicode form while `normalize()`/`equal()` still behave as though canonicalization happened. Two URLs that Node's WHATWG parser would consider identical can compare unequal in fast-uri (and vice versa).

**Dependency chain (`pnpm-lock.yaml`):**
```
ajv@8.18.0 > fast-uri@3.1.2
```
`ajv@8.18.0` is a direct dependency; `new Ajv2020()` is instantiated in `src/services/workshop/validator.ts:48`.

title: CVE-2026-16221 in fast-uri 3.1.2 via ajv (URL security-policy bypass — backslash not treated as authority delimiter)
description: The transitive package **`fast-uri@3.1.2`** (pinned via `pnpm-lock.yaml` through `ajv`) is affected by CVE-2026-16221: versions 2.3.1 through 4.1.0 do not treat a literal backslash (U+005C) as an authority delimiter, whereas Node's native WHATWG URL parser (used by `fetch`, `undici`, `http`) normalizes `\` to `/` for special schemes. A URL that ajv/fast-uri validates as one origin can resolve to a different host at fetch time, bypassing URI-format/security policy. Fixed in `3.1.4` / `4.1.1` / `2.4.3`.
impact: An attacker-supplied URL containing a backslash (e.g. `https://allowed.com\\.evil.com/`) is parsed by fast-uri as belonging to the allowed origin, while Node's WHATWG parser used at fetch time treats the backslash as a path separator and sends the request to `evil.com`. This bypasses origin/host security policy with Integrity impact only.
technical_analysis:
**Root cause:** fast-uri ≤ 4.1.0 (3.x to 3.1.3) does not treat `\` as an authority delimiter; WHATWG URL treats it as equivalent to `/` for special schemes. Validation-vs-resolution disagreement.

**Dependency chain (`pnpm-lock.yaml`):** `ajv@8.18.0 > fast-uri@3.1.2`. `ajv@8.18.0` is direct (package.json), instantiated at `src/services/workshop/validator.ts:48`.

**Root cause:** fast-uri < 3.1.5 / 4.1.2 / 2.4.4 requires literal `//` for an authority; a `\`-introduced authority is folded into the path, but the WHATWG parser keeps the authority. Validation and resolution disagree on the effective host.

title: Missing authorization on global audit log endpoints — any authenticated user can read the full system audit trail
description: The global audit-log endpoints **`GET /api/v1/audit/log`**, **`GET /api/v1/audit/log/:executionId`**, and **`GET /api/v1/audit/stats`** are protected only by the global authentication middleware (any valid Keycloak JWT) with **no role or permission check**. A principal with zero business roles can enumerate the entire security/compliance audit trail — 21,252+ entries exposing every user's `executedBy` ID, `sourceIp`, action parameters, and error details.
impact: Any authenticated principal, including an account with no assigned business roles (`realm_access.roles = ['offline_access','marking:PUBLIC','default-roles-tellus']`), can read the complete cross-user audit trail. The PoC returned **21,252 audit entries** containing other users' internal user UUIDs (`executedBy`), client IPs (`sourceIp`), and full business parameters of their actions (loan application primary keys such as `QA-RW-BK-L-0000048`, credit-decision `rationale` and `approvedLimit` values, results, and error messages). The file header for this route states the audit log is "legally mandatory — every data modification must be traceable", i.e. it is compliance/security data intended for administrators and auditors only. This is a privacy and regulatory exposure (mass disclosure of who did what, when, from where, across the whole system), and it also aids further attacks by revealing valid object primary keys, user IDs, and internal error details.
technical_analysis:
The three global audit handlers invoke the audit query path directly, with no authorization middleware between the router and the handler. `globalAuditRouter.get` is called with only a path and the async handler:

```typescript title=src/routes/auditLog.ts startLineNumber=280 endLineNumber=282
globalAuditRouter.get(
  "/log",
  async (req: Request, res: Response, next: NextFunction) => {
```

The router is mounted in `src/server.ts` with no guard either: `app.use("/api/v1/audit", globalAuditRouter);`. The `globalAuth` middleware applied earlier in the stack only verifies that a valid JWT is present (authentication); it performs no role/permission evaluation. Per the project's own route-map analysis, "Routes with NO route-level authz beyond globalAuth: POST /api/v1/sql, /api/v1/audit." The SQL built by `queryAuditLog()` is parameterized (no SQL injection), so the issue is purely the missing function-level authorization. The same codebase already demonstrates the correct pattern: `POST /api/v1/sql/invalidate` in `src/routes/sql.ts` is wrapped with `authorize('ontology-admin')` imported from `src/middleware/auth.ts`.

## Summary

The global audit-log endpoints (`GET /api/v1/audit/log`, `GET /api/v1/audit/log/:executionId`, `GET /api/v1/audit/stats`) were reachable by any authenticated JWT — including principals with zero business roles — because the handlers were registered with no authorization middleware. title: IDOR: authenticated users read arbitrary projects and dataset file contents (dataset RBAC disabled by default + default-org auto-enroll voids project read isolation)
description: The Ontology Engine's dataset read endpoints (`GET /api/v1/datasets/:datasetId`, `/preview`, `/download`, `/status`, `/summary`) and project read endpoints (`GET /api/v1/projects/:id`, `/:id/stats`, `/:id/folders`, `/:id/datasets/all`, `/:id/members`) enforce no object-level authorization. Any authenticated user — even one with zero roles and no project membership — can read arbitrary projects and exfiltrate the full contents of any uploaded dataset file by direct object ID (IDOR / Broken Object-Level Authorization). Only write operations are correctly gated.
impact: Full contents of any uploaded dataset file are readable cross-user by any holder of a valid bearer token. Project metadata (owner, members' emails/roles), folder trees, datasets lists, stats, and summaries for arbitrary projects are likewise exposed. Confidentiality of all stored file data is broken; only integrity is preserved because write paths (PUT/DELETE project, POST folder/members, upload) correctly return 403/404 for the same actor. No special role, project membership, or org sharing is required beyond authentication.
technical_analysis:
Root cause is two-part.

**Part A — dataset by-id reads have no object-level authorization by default.**
`src/routes/foundryDatasets.ts:36` mounts `datasetRouter.use(dataPlaneGuard({ post: 'write' }))`. In `src/middleware/requireRole.ts:150-160`, `dataPlaneGuard` short-circuits ALL GET/HEAD/OPTIONS with an immediate `next()` — it only gates DELETE (ontology-admin) and POST/PUT/PATCH (ontology-write). Reads therefore pass with no principal/object binding. The only object-level guard is `requireDatasetRole('viewer')` on routes lines 43-50, but it is OPT-IN: `src/services/datasetAcl.ts:208-209` `isDatasetRbacEnabled()` returns true only when `process.env.DATASET_RBAC_ENABLED === 'true'`; it defaults to `"false"` and is not set in `.env` or any docker-compose file. When disabled the middleware no-ops (`if (!isDatasetRbacEnabled()) return next();`). Net effect: dataset reads are authenticated-but-unauthorized → IDOR.

**Part B — the project/folder membership read-boundary is a no-op.**
`src/services/projectService.ts:127-129` `listProjects` and `:146-160` `getProjectById` use `orgSharedProjects()` / an EXISTS subquery joining `project_organizations`↔`user_organizations`. But `src/foundryMigrate.ts` (B4 Step 19 backfill ~1264-1271 and Step 19b auto-enroll triggers ~1289-1315) seeds ONE shared org `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001` ("default") and auto-enrolls EVERY user and EVERY project into it via `enroll_user_default_org()` and `enroll_project_default_org()` AFTER INSERT triggers. The org-membership EXISTS predicate is therefore trivially true for every (user, project) pair — "org-shared read" is effectively global read, and project-based reads (`/folders`, `/datasets/all`, `/members`, `/stats`) inherit it.

Writes remain correctly gated by `authorizeRoles('owner'/'editor')` and `owner_id` checks in ProjectService/FolderService, confirming the read-side org shortcut was never meant to be the enforcement point.

Both a zero-role user (`cypress-nogroups@tellus.local`, realm_access.roles = only `offline_access` + `default-roles-tellus`, not in `project_members`, in no legitimate shared org) and a `marking:PUBLIC`-viewer context were validated; the IDOR reproduces for both against the admin's private project `f33e3cec-2676-416f-a095-04e3de11f2ed`.

## Harden system-status endpoints against unauthenticated disclosure

**Problem.** `GET /api/v1/system/health` and `GET /health/detailed` answer without any credentials and return the PostgreSQL version, per-table row counts, the live OpenSearch cluster name/node count, all index names with document counts and sizes, the full object-type inventory (apiName / propertyCount / objectCount / lastIndexed / indexStatus), process memory footprint and uptime. ## Require authentication for the OpenAPI spec and Swagger UI

**Problem.** `GET /api/docs/spec.json` (616 KB, 612 paths) and the Swagger UI at `/api/docs` are reachable without authentication. The generated spec catalogues the entire privileged surface — user administration (`/api/v1/auth/admin/users` create/delete/enable/invite), role and member CRUD, OAuth application registration, settings read/write, and function-publish grant/audit administration (`/api/v1/functions/admin/*`). Because the spec is derived from the live route table, it is always complete and current — an ideal adversary reconnaissance artifact.

**Fix.**
- `src/middleware/globalAuth.ts`: remove `/api/docs` from the unauthenticated allowlist so the family requires a valid JWT like every other API path.

**Problem.** `/api/metrics`, `/api/v1/pipelines/metrics`, and `/api/v1/funnel/metrics` are unauthenticated on the documented assumption that "scrape targets are internal-only (network isolation, not JWT)". title: BFLA: zero-role remote users manage superadmin function-publish grants and self-escalate to function-publish code execution (CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH dev fallback reachable behind proxy)
description: The function-publish admin surface (`/api/v1/functions/admin/*`) is protected by `requireSuperadmin`, but the upstream authentication middleware fabricates a superadmin principal for any request that appears to come from localhost. Because the deployment sits behind a gateway/proxy, `req.socket.remoteAddress` is loopback for all callers, so any authenticated remote user — even one with zero platform roles — can list, create, and revoke function-publish grants. A zero-role user can therefore grant itself a global function-publish grant and reach arbitrary TypeScript function-publish code execution (Broken Function-Level Authorization → privilege escalation → RCE).
impact: Any holder of a valid JWT for any user can manage superadmin-only publish grants: list all grants and the publish audit log, create arbitrary grants, and revoke other principals' grants. By creating a `global` grant bound to its own `keycloak_sub`, a zero-role user satisfies `authorizePublish()` in `services/functions/executionPolicy.ts` (~lines 368-374) and can then publish and execute arbitrary TypeScript functions through the worker_threads+vm executor pool (`src/services/functionExecutor.ts`, documented as not a security boundary). This is a full self-driven privilege escalation from a plain authenticated user to remote code execution, plus the ability to disrupt others by revoking their grants (Availability). Confirmed up to an active global grant; the publish step itself was not executed.
technical_analysis:
Mount chain: `server.ts:1044` mounts `app.use("/api/v1/functions/admin", createFunctionPublishAdminRouter({ pool }))`; the router applies `router.use(requireCodeReposAuth())` at `services/functions/admin/routes.ts:194`, and each handler (`routes.ts:81-92`, the GET list at `routes.ts:431-434`, plus `:209`/`:565`) correctly calls `requireSuperadmin(req, res)`. The authorization check itself is present — the failure is in the principal that reaches it.

`src/services/codeRepos/middleware/principal.ts` `requireCodeReposAuth()`: when `isTestAuthBypassEnabled("CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH")` is true and NO `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header is present, it falls to the "localhost dev fallback" (lines ~166-191). `isLocalhost(req)` (line ~69) checks only `req.socket.remoteAddress ∈ {127.0.0.1, ::1, ::ffff:127.0.0.1}`. Behind the deployment's gateway/proxy, the app sees a loopback-ish peer for every caller, so remote users satisfy it and are handed `DEV_FALLBACK_PRINCIPAL = "53cf9bcf-4c20-4aed-83f4-3c7e405453b4/OWNER,EDITOR,READER,tellus-superadmin"` (lines 80-81) — the admin's real Keycloak `sub` plus `tellus-superadmin` — without presenting any credential beyond an arbitrary valid Keycloak JWT. `requireSuperadmin` then sees `tellus-superadmin` and passes.

Config: `.env:137` sets `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1`; `docker-compose.override.yml:33` defaults it to 0 but `.env` is the loaded value; `utils/testAuthGate.ts` only fails closed when `NODE_ENV==="production"`, and the running app has `NODE_ENV=development`. The whole bypass chain is therefore ACTIVE in this deployment and in any environment with `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1` + non-production `NODE_ENV` + a localhost-appearing proxy.

Attacker verified: `cypress-nogroups@tellus.local` (`sub bcd2551e-b985-4d6f-97ff-e0e087a87e20`, realm roles only `offline_access` + `default-roles-tellus`, zero platform roles), no `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header sent. Contrast: repeating the request with a crafted `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` carrying `roles:[]` returns HTTP 403 `Functions:PermissionDenied superadmin-required` — proving `requireSuperadmin` works and that the bypass comes from the fabricated-principal fallback, not a missing check.

title: Stored XSS / Active Content via Attachment Upload (inline content-disposition, cross-user readable)
description: The v2 attachment upload endpoint accepts user-supplied files with arbitrary filenames and MIME types, stores them verbatim, and the content endpoint serves them back with `Content-Disposition: inline` and the stored `Content-Type`. An authenticated low-privilege user can upload `text/html` or `image/svg+xml` content that any other authenticated user's browser renders in-line when fetched. Cross-user read succeeds (viewer's attachment is served to an admin), and although CSP blocks inline JavaScript, active content is still rendered, enabling phishing UI and CSS-based exfiltration of DOM data.
impact: Any authenticated low-privilege user can store renderer-active content (HTML/SVG) that is served inline to other authenticated users who know or can guess the attachment rid, enabling phishing UI, cross-origin CSS-based exfiltration of in-page sensitive data, and external-resource tracking of victims — despite CSP blocking inline JavaScript.
technical_analysis:
`POST /api/v2/ontologies/attachments/upload?filename=...` (raw bytes) stores the uploaded file in object storage and records the client-supplied `filename` and a `Content-Type` (either the request's declared `Content-Type` or extension sniff via `mediaTypeForFilename`). There is **no allowlist** restricting which media types may be stored, so `text/html`, `image/svg+xml`, etc. are accepted.

`GET /api/v2/ontologies/attachments/:rid/content` (`src/routes/v2/attachmentsV2.ts`) then does:

```typescript title=src/routes/v2/attachmentsV2.ts startLineNumber=80 endLineNumber=85
res.setHeader("Content-Type", result.row.media_type);
res.setHeader("Content-Length", result.row.size_bytes);
res.setHeader(
  "Content-Disposition",
  `inline; filename="${encodeURIComponent(result.row.filename)}"`,
);
```

Serving `text/html` / `image/svg+xml` with `inline` disposition renders the bytes as active content in the fetching user's browser. Because there is no per-user authorization check on `getAttachmentContent`, any authenticated principal who learns the (unpredictable) attachment rid can fetch another user's attachment. The rid is the only "authorization" (a capability-by-secrecy pattern), which is a defense-in-depth weakness.

CSP is `default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; script-src-attr 'none'`, so inline `<script>` / event handlers are blocked (verified: `onerror=alert(1337)` did not fire). However:
- `style-src 'self' https: 'unsafe-inline'` permits inline `<style>`, and the browser fetches the declaration URLs cross-origin → **CSS-based exfiltration of DOM data** (attribute selectors) was demonstrated: a `<div data-secret="...">` and `<input value="...">` leaked their starting characters to attacker-controlled URLs via `background:url(...)`.
- `form-action 'self'` blocks external form POSTs, but `text/html` still renders arbitrary UI (phishing overlays, navigatable via SVG `<a>`).
- SVG `<image href="https://...">` loads external resources → tracking/active rendering.

Verified live: viewer uploads `text/html` attachment; admin fetches `/api/v2/ontologies/attachments/<rid>/content` and receives `200`, `Content-Type: text/html`, `Content-Disposition: inline; filename="t.html"`; the HTML is parsed into the DOM (screenshot + outerHTML confirmed rendering, and a `<style>`-based exfil request was issued cross-origin).

remediation_steps:
1. Enforce an allowlist of safe media types on upload (e.g., images minus SVG, plain text, PDF) and reject or normalize `text/html`, `image/svg+xml`, `application/xhtml+xml`, and any `text/*` that is not plain text.
2. Serve attachments with `Content-Disposition: attachment` (force download) and always a safe, computed `Content-Type` (never trust the client-declared type); add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (already present) plus a restrictive per-response CSP such as `sandbox` / `default-src 'none'` for active types that must be previewed.

Previously any authenticated user could store `text/html`/`image/svg+xml` and the content endpoint served it back inline with the stored Content-Type, so a victim fetching the attachment URL would render attacker-supplied HTML/SVG in-line (CSP blocks inline JS, but `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` still permits active content such as cross-origin CSS exfiltration and phishing UI). The new `safeAttachmentContentType` guard downgrades renderer-active types at the serving boundary; a follow-up should also enforce the same allowlist at upload time and add per-resource authorization instead of relying on rid secrecy.

title: IDOR: Cross-user read of Quiver AIP traces exposes LLM prompts and tool inputs
description: The `GET /quiver/api/v1/aip/traces/:rid` endpoint returns any user's AIP trace — including the plaintext `prompt` and `toolInvocations` — to any other authenticated user. The ownership check on `src/routes/quiver/aip.ts` contains an empty enforcement block, so it never actually rejects a mismatched caller.
impact: Any authenticated user (including the lowest-privilege "viewer" role and zero-role accounts) can read every other user's Quiver AIP traces. Traces contain the full plaintext LLM prompt — which in real usage embeds business data, object rids, and PII (e.g. "show quarterly revenue for confidential clients") — plus complete tool-invocation inputs. The trace rid is disclosed in the SSE `done` frame of every AIP call, so discovery of another user's rid is trivial for any co-tenant attacker. This is a horizontal, cross-user confidentiality breach of AI-assistant conversation content. Demonstrated impact is read of a single other user's trace (C:L); prompt content is stored plaintext so leakage is direct, not hashed.

title: Design flaw: client-controlled authorizeApplyAction flag bypasses the OMS authorization gate for the privileged apply_action LLM tool
description: The Quiver AIP routes decide whether the privileged `apply_action` tool appears in the LLM's authorized manifest based solely on a client-supplied `authorizeApplyAction` boolean in the request body. This bypasses the intended server-side OMS `canApplyAction` check, so any authenticated user can claim authorization to the privileged tool. Live execution of the action is not demonstrated on the current in-process mock backend, so the impact is latent/design-level — but the same route will trust the same flag when the production AIP service is wired in.
impact: The authorization decision for the most privileged AIP tool (`apply_action` — deterministic ontology action execution) is client-controlled at the HTTP boundary. A low-privilege authenticated user can self-authorize the tool simply by sending `"authorizeApplyAction": true`, and the orchestrator will accept `apply_action` tool calls from the LLM against that forged manifest. On the current in-process mock backend this does not reach a real action execution (the backend does not invoke actions and a test guard intercepts the proposal), so the demonstrated impact today is the ability to manipulate the tool manifest and obtain privileged-tool proposals the user's role should not allow — a compromised authorization boundary rather than a proven write. The flaw is critical to fix before the production `tellus-aip-logic-service` is connected, because the identical route and flag would then gate real action execution.
poc_description:
1. Mint a JWT for a low-privilege user (viewer) with no OMS action-apply grants on the analysis.
2. Call `POST /quiver/api/v1/aip/generate` with `"authorizeApplyAction": true` in the body.
3. Observe that the request is accepted and the orchestrator runs with `apply_action` in the authorized manifest (i.e. the manifest gate was satisfied by the client flag rather than by a server-side `canApplyAction` decision).
4. Confirm, from `src/routes/quiver/aip.ts` and `src/services/quiver/aip/tools.ts`, that the intended `buildAuthorizedManifest` / `AuthPort.canApplyAction` path is never invoked by the route.
poc_script_code:
# Low-privilege viewer self-authorizes the privileged apply_action tool
KC=http://host.docker.internal:8086/realms/tellus/protocol/openid-connect/token
VIEWER=$(curl -s -X POST "$KC" -H "Host: localhost:8086" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "grant_type=password&client_id=tellus-frontend&username=cypress-viewer@tellus.local&password=Password123!&scope=openid" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys;print(json.load(sys.stdin)['access_token'])")

curl -s -X POST http://host.docker.internal:3000/quiver/api/v1/aip/generate \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VIEWER" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"analysisRid":"ri.analysis.probe.1","prompt":"...","authorizeApplyAction":true}'
# The route appends "apply_action" to authorizedTools solely because of the
# client-supplied boolean; AuthPort.canApplyAction is never consulted at the route.
remediation_steps: Do not let a client field decide tool authorization. Remove `authorizeApplyAction` from the public request schemas (or accept it only on paths explicitly gated by the Quiver test-auth bypass), and have the route build the authorized tool set via the existing `buildAuthorizedManifest` in `tools.ts`, resolving the `candidateActionTypeRid` server-side from the analysis context and calling `AuthPort.canApplyAction` for the real user before `apply_action` is ever added to the manifest. The same fix must be kept when the production `tellus-aip-logic-service` replaces the in-process mock. Add a regression test asserting `authorizeApplyAction: true` from an unprivileged user does not result in an authorized `apply_action` manifest entry.
assumptions: Assumes the deployed stack with the in-process mock AIP backend (`NODE_ENV=development` as deployed). Full live execution of a real ontology action was not demonstrated: the mock backend does not invoke actions and its test guard raises `Tellus:Quiver:LlmToolUnauthorized` before a proposal propagates, so no Integrity-high impact is claimed. The attacker is a legitimately authenticated low-privilege user. The finding's weight is that the authorization boundary at the route is already wrong and will gate real execution once the production AIP service is wired in.

code_locations.label: Replace client-flag tool authorization with server-side manifest build

fix_pr_body:
## Summary

The Quiver AIP routes (`generate` / `configure` / `assist`) decide whether the privileged `apply_action` tool is offered to the LLM from a client-supplied `authorizeApplyAction` boolean. The intended server-side gate — `buildAuthorizedManifest` in `services/quiver/aip/tools.ts`, which retains `apply_action` only when `AuthPort.canApplyAction` succeeds for a server-resolved `candidateActionTypeRid` — is never called by the route. `orchestrator.ts` then authorizes tool calls purely against this request-derived manifest.

## Impact

Any authenticated user can add `apply_action` to their authorized manifest by sending `"authorizeApplyAction": true`. On the current in-process mock backend this does not reach real action execution, but the authorization boundary is already wrong and would gate live action execution once the production `tellus-aip-logic-service` is connected. Fix before the production backend is wired in.

## Fix

Stop deriving tool authorization from a client field: remove `authorizeApplyAction` from the public request schemas (or confine it to test-auth-bypassed paths), resolve the `candidateActionTypeRid` server-side from the analysis, and route the manifest through `buildAuthorizedManifest` so `apply_action` is present only after a real `AuthPort.canApplyAction` decision. Add a regression test that a low-privilege user setting the flag cannot obtain an authorized `apply_action` manifest entry.

title: Pre-auth test-auth bypass grants attacker-controlled tellus-superadmin via X-Tellus-Test-Auth header (globalAuth)
description: The global authentication gate honors the `X-Tellus-Test-Auth` header and `Authorization: Bearer test-auth:...` whenever `NODE_ENV !== 'production'` and `TELLUS_TEST_HOOKS=1`, with **no source-address restriction**. The role list embedded in the header is copied verbatim into the fabricated principal, so an unauthenticated remote caller can assert `tellus-superadmin` (and `marking:TOP_SECRET`, `ontology-admin`) on every request. This yields full unauthenticated administrative access to the API.
impact: Any remote unauthenticated attacker becomes `tellus-superadmin` (and `marking:TOP_SECRET`), bypassing all Keycloak authentication and role authorization on every route protected by globalAuth. Demonstrated: `X-Tellus-Test-Auth: <uuid>:tellus-superadmin,ontology-admin,marking:TOP_SECRET` returns HTTP 200 with object-type data, and the same header gains access to superadmin-only grant management. Full confidentiality and integrity loss of the ontology.
poc_description:
1. From any host that can reach the API (no credentials, no source code), send an authenticated-read request with no headers and observe HTTP 401.
2. Repeat the same request adding `X-Tellus-Test-Auth: <any-uuid>:tellus-superadmin,ontology-admin,marking:TOP_SECRET` and observe HTTP 200 with protected data.
3. Repeat the same with the `Authorization: Bearer test-auth:<any-uuid>:tellus-superadmin` header form and observe HTTP 200.
4. Hit a superadmin-only route (e.g. GET /api/v1/functions/admin/function-publish-grants) with the same header and observe HTTP 200.
poc_script_code:
```bash
APP=http://host.docker.internal:3000

# Control: without any credential the API correctly rejects.
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' $APP/api/v1/ontology/default/objectTypes   # -> 401

# Bypass 1 — arbitrary user + superadmin roles, no token at all.
curl -s -o /tmp/b1.json -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  -H "X-Tellus-Test-Auth: deadbeef-0000-0000-0000-000000000001:tellus-superadmin,ontology-admin,marking:TOP_SECRET" \
  $APP/api/v1/ontology/default/objectTypes   # -> 200
head -c 200 /tmp/b1.json

# Bypass 2 — same via the Bearer 'test-auth:' form.
curl -s -o /tmp/b2.json -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer test-auth:cafebabe-1111-2222-3333-444455556666:tellus-superadmin" \
  $APP/api/v1/ontology/default/objectTypes   # -> 200

# Superadmin-only endpoint is reachable with the fabricated roles.
curl -s -o /tmp/b3.json -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  -H "X-Tellus-Test-Auth: deadbeef-0000-0000-0000-000000000001:tellus-superadmin" \
  $APP/api/v1/functions/admin/function-publish-grants   # -> 200 with grant rows
```
remediation_steps:
1. Never honor test-principal headers on network-reachable deployments. Move the entire test-auth bypass out of `globalAuth`’s request path and behind an explicit, source-address-and-environment guard.
2. Require BOTH `NODE_ENV` to be a non-production value **and** a distinct, rotation-capable shared secret (e.g. `TELLUS_TEST_HOOKS_SECRET`) that must accompany any test-auth assertion — never the flag alone.
3. Add a source-address check (loopback only) mirroring `isLocalhost()` in `principal.ts` to both bypass branches in `globalAuth`; do not allow the header path to be more permissive than the code-repos fallback.
4. Stop copying request-supplied roles verbatim; the principal builder should only accept a fixed allowlist of test users from `TEST_USER_SEEDS`, not arbitrary `userId`/role strings.
5. Add a boot-time assertion that fails startup when `TELLUS_TEST_HOOKS=1` and the server is bound to a non-loopback interface, independent of `NODE_ENV`.

title: Unauthenticated remote publication of executable TypeScript Functions via dev test-auth fallback
description: The publish gate that protects the non-sandboxed worker_threads+vm Function executor (`POST /api/v1/functions/:repositoryRid/versions`) is bypassable from the network with no credentials. When `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1` is active and the request carries no `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header, `requireCodeReposAuth()` substitutes a hard-coded dev fallback principal whose `userId` already holds a **global** `function_publish_grants` row; `authorizePublish()` then admits the caller via `db_grant`. A forged `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header that simply names the realm role `function:publish` also yields publish rights via `keycloak_role`. Both paths create immutable, executable function-version rows in the Functions registry with no authentication.
impact: An unauthenticated network attacker can write arbitrary TypeScript artifacts into the Functions registry (the platform's executable-code store) under semver tags of their choosing. This defeats the security boundary documented in `src/services/executionPolicy.ts` and `src/services/functionExecutor.ts` — the executor is explicitly *not* a sandbox (worker_threads + Node `vm`), so publication is the only control preventing untrusted code from reaching the runtime. The demonstrated impact is an unauthorized **integrity** violation: the attacker can plant and version executable code (immutable, content-addressed, so it cannot be overwritten — confirmed HTTP 409 on re-POST with different sha256). This is the enabling step for the documented (but not demonstrated in this test) follow-on risk of remote code execution inside the API container. No confidentiality or availability impact was demonstrated; the runtime sandbox rejected `process`/`Function`-based escape probes during a safe invocation attempt.
technical_analysis:
Two independent paths in `requireCodeReposAuth()` (src/services/codeRepos/middleware/principal.ts) let an unauthenticated caller become an authorized publisher:

1. **Dev-fallback substitution (no header)** — When `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1` and no `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header is present, and the TCP peer is classified as localhost, the middleware replaces the request's principal with `DEV_FALLBACK_PRINCIPAL = "53cf9bcf-4c20-4aed-83f4-3c7e405453b4/OWNER,EDITOR,READER,tellus-superadmin"`. Requests from the sandbox arrive via the Docker gateway and satisfy the `isLocalhost()` check, so the substitution fires for *remote* callers. The hard-coded `userId` `53cf9bcf-...` has a pre-existing global `function_publish_grants` row (seeded on 2026-08-08 with reason "local dev fallback principal (CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH dev mode)"), so `authorizePublish()` admits the request with `decision_source = db_grant`. The audit row records the fallback identity, not the caller's — cross-user attribution is broken.

2. **Forged header** — `applyHeaderPrincipal()` passes roles from `X-Tellus-Test-Principal: <userId>/<role>` verbatim into `principal.roles`. `authorizePublish()` step (a) checks `roles.includes(policy.publishRole)` where `publishRole = "function:publish"`, so a header value of `<any-uuid>/function:publish` yields publish rights via `decision_source = keycloak_role`. No Keycloak signature or role assignment is consulted.

The authorization model itself (`executionPolicy.ts`) is otherwise robust: a forged principal **without** the `function:publish` role is denied (403 `Functions:PermissionDenied`), and the artifact-integrity controls are sound (re-publishing the same semver with a different sha256 returns HTTP 409 `Functions:VersionImmutable`). Live config: `NODE_ENV=development`, `TELLUS_TEST_HOOKS=1`, `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1`, `FUNCTION_EXECUTION_TRUST_MODE` unset → `trusted-authors-only`. No Keycloak user (including superadmin) is assigned the `function:publish` realm role — verification of the JWTs `realm_access.roles` — so the *only* admission paths are the two above, both of which are attacker-controlled. The `globalAuth.ts` allowlist (lines 195, 210) permits unauthenticated traffic to reach the per-router middleware, exposing the bypass.
poc_description:

## Summary
Removes the unauthenticated Function publication bypass by (1) deleting the implicit dev-fallback principal substitution, and (2) adding a defense-in-depth deny for synthetic/test principals in the DB-grant path of `authorizePublish()`.

## Root cause
When `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1` and no `X-Tellus-Test-Principal` header is sent, `requireCodeReposAuth()` replaced the request identity with a hard-coded fallback whose `userId` owns a **global** `function_publish_grants` row, yielding `db_grant` publish rights to any caller whose TCP peer looks like localhost (Docker gateway traffic qualifies). Separately, the header path passes roles verbatim into the principal, so a forged header naming `function:publish` yields `keycloak_role` publish rights.

- `src/services/codeRepos/middleware/principal.ts` — delete the `DEV_FALLBACK_PRINCIPAL` constant and the `applyHeaderPrincipal(..., DEV_FALLBACK_PRINCIPAL)` substitution; unauthenticated requests now 401.
- `src/services/functions/executionPolicy.ts` — `authorizePublish()` refuses the `db_grant` path when the caller's `source` is `test`, so even if a synthetic principal again reaches the gate, a grants row cannot authorize it.
- Migration (not included): revoke the existing global grant for subject `53cf9bcf-4c20-4aed-83f4-3c7e405453b4` and assert no grants exist for test/fallback subjects.

- Integration test: `POST /api/v1/functions/:rid/versions` with no auth returns 401.

title: IPv6 Literal Canonicalisation Mismatch Permanently Blocks Webhook Delivery to IPv6 REST Source Hosts
description: The connectivity webhook executor rejects any call whose REST source domain is an IPv6 literal because two layers of the stack normalise the host differently: WHATWG `URL.hostname` keeps the brackets (`[::1]`) while the connection's persisted egress-allowlist host entry stores the bare literal (`::1`). `assertConnectionAllows` (executor.ts:414-421) does a verbatim `entry.host.toLowerCase() === hostname.toLowerCase()` and throws `EGRESS_POLICY_BLOCKED` before any socket is opened. A connection whose ONLY approved target is the IPv6 host therefore can never execute any webhook — the user-approved egress policy is unreachable, breaking the feature and silently preventing legitimate automation for any IPv6-addressed internal REST source (the exact deployment shape the `::1` / ULA / link-local entries in `CONNECTIVITY_EGRESS_ALLOW_RESERVED` exist to support).
impact: Loss of availability for the affected integration path. An operator who configures a REST source domain as an IPv6 literal (loopback `::1`, ULA `fc00::/7`, link-local `fe80::/10`, or IPv4-mapped `::ffff:a.b.c.d`) can create the connection, pass validation, pass the per-connection egress-allowlist, and still have every webhook invocation fail with `EGRESS_POLICY_BLOCKED`. The failure is silent to the operator: no configuration error is surfaced at create time, and the runtime error message (`The source egress policy does not allow [::1]:9000`) incorrectly blames the policy rather than the canonicalisation bug. Because the feature is intended to support IPv6 internal targets (as evidenced by `CONNECTIVITY_EGRESS_ALLOW_RESERVED` explicitly allowing `::1` hostnames), this is a feature-breakage defect, not a data-disclosure or authorisation bypass.
technical_analysis:
`executeCall` (src/services/connectivity/webhooks/executor.ts:776) resolves the URL:

```typescript
const url = new URL(path, base);
```

WHATWG URL spec returns `url.hostname` for an IPv6 literal WITH brackets, e.g. `"[::1]"`. `assertConnectionAllows` (same file, lines 410-425) compares that against `entry.host.toLowerCase()` where `entry.host` comes from the connection's `egressPolicy.allowlist`. The connection's allowlist entry was validated at create-time by `EgressEntry` (src/services/connectivity/contracts.ts:181-185) as `z.string().min(1)` — no canonicalisation. An operator writes `::1`; the executor compares `"[::1]" === "::1"` → false → `EGRESS_POLICY_BLOCKED` thrown at executor.ts:813.

The same code path is hit for every IPv6-literal `baseUrl`. Hostname-based (non-literal) and all IPv4-literal domains are unaffected, so the bug is invisible in the common case. A second, identical mismatch exists at executor.ts:1143 where `safePolicy.allowedHosts` is pre-normalised from the same raw entries — after fixing `assertConnectionAllows`, the same request would then hit `assertEgressUrl`'s `FORBIDDEN_HOST` check against a raw `::1` entry while the URL hostname is `[::1]`. Both sites must be canonicalised for the gate to work end-to-end.

The audit note in the connectivity code refers to "hostname case-insensitivity" but not to bracket canonicalisation; no unit test covers an IPv6-literal domain. The PostgreSQL connector already handles this correctly (`isEgressAllowed` in postgresql/egress.ts strips brackets via `replace(/^\[/,"").replace(/\]$/,"")`) — the webhook executor was the only outbound path that did not.

## Summary
Fix IPv6 literal canonicalisation mismatch in the connectivity webhook executor that permanently blocks webhook delivery to any IPv6-addressed REST source domain.

## Problem
WHATWG `URL.hostname` preserves brackets for IPv6 literals (`[::1]`), but the connection's persisted egress-allowlist stores the bare literal (`::1`). `assertConnectionAllows` and the `allowedHosts` projection in `executeWebhook` both compared these two different forms verbatim, so the policy gate always failed with `EGRESS_POLICY_BLOCKED` before any socket was opened. Any connection whose only approved target is an IPv6 host could never execute a webhook.

## Fix
Strip one pair of surrounding square brackets from both sides of the comparison in `assertConnectionAllows` (executor.ts:414-421) and when projecting the allowlist into `safePolicy.allowedHosts` (executor.ts:1142-1145). Matches the existing idiom in `postgresql/egress.ts::isReservedTarget`.

## Verification
- Pre-fix: `EGRESS_POLICY_BLOCKED` ("does not allow [::1]:9000").
- After first patch: error advances to `EGRESS_URL_BLOCKED` from the next gate, proving the first comparison now passes.
- After second patch: the request reaches the DNS/transport layer (source inspection confirms no remaining raw `.map((entry) => entry.host.toLowerCase())` sites in the executor).
- The PostgreSQL connector already handles this correctly and is unchanged.

title: Internal Service Fingerprinting via Rate-Limit-Exempt PostgreSQL Connectivity Probe (/api/v1/connectivity/connections/test-config)
description: `POST /api/v1/connectivity/connections/test-config` opens a real TCP socket to a caller-supplied `host:port` and returns response envelopes whose error-class deterministically distinguishes a **closed port** (`502 Tellus:Connectivity:JdbcConnectFailed`), an **open non-PostgreSQL port** (`500 InternalError "Connection terminated unexpectedly"`), an **open PostgreSQL port** (`401 Tellus:Connectivity:JdbcAuthFailed`), and a **firewalled / non-answering service** (`500 InternalError "Connection terminated due to connection timeout"` after ~5 s). The route's `testRateLimit` middleware deliberately exempts every authenticated principal from the request rate limit, so any authenticated caller holding the `connectivity:test` scope can sweep loopback and any operator-allowlisted address space at full speed and enumerate internal services by port, protocol family, and reachability.
impact: An authenticated, connectivity-privileged attacker learns the internal service inventory (which TCP services exist on loopback and any operator-allowlisted hosts, which speak PostgreSQL, and which are slow/blackhole) without needing network-level access to those segments. On the verified stack this fingerprinted the Express app (3000), the frontend (3001), PostgreSQL (5432), Temporal gRPC (7233), and non-answering services on 9000 (MinIO), 8086 (Keycloak), 6379 (Redis), and 9200 (OpenSearch). This is internal service metadata disclosure that materially assists targeting for every other finding, but it does not itself expose application data or allow modification — hence Confidentiality impact is limited (C:L) and Integrity/Availability are unaffected.
technical_analysis:
`src/services/connectivity/handlers/test.handler.ts` `testConfig` (~line 310): after `assertEgressResolved` allows the target (the dev stack sets `CONNECTIVITY_EGRESS_ALLOW_RESERVED=localhost,127.0.0.1/8,::1`; the equivalent operator allowlist plays the same role in any deployment), the handler builds a one-shot `pg.Pool` and awaits `SELECT version()` within a 5 s probe budget. `mapPgError` classifies the pg driver's outcome into `auth` / `connect` / `other`, and the error mapping then emits a **different HTTP envelope per outcome**:

- closed port (`ECONNREFUSED` etc.) → `502 Tellus:Connectivity:JdbcConnectFailed`
- TCP connected but not a PG server → `500 InternalError "Connection terminated unexpectedly"`
- PG server that rejects the credentials (`28P01`/`28000`) → `401 Tellus:Connectivity:JdbcAuthFailed`
- TCP connect hangs / no reply within the budget → `500 InternalError "Connection terminated due to connection timeout"` (5 s)

That four-way distinction is a clean oracle: status + `errorName` + message reveal whether a socket succeeded and what kind of service answered. The egress *blocker* (`assertEgressForConfig` / `assertEgressResolved`) correctly refuses reserved targets that are not allowlisted, so the residual issue is the **response-side oracle on allowed targets**, not the guard.

Separately, `testRateLimit` (lines 60-104) short-circuits with `next()` for any request whose bearer token resolves to a principal:

```
if (principalId && process.env.CONNECTIVITY_TEST_RATE_LIMIT_ALL !== "1") {
    next();           // authenticated → exempt from the 6/min token bucket
    return;
}
```

so the only velocity bound on the sweep is disabled by default for exactly the attackers who can authenticate. Combined, an authenticated principal with `connectivity:test` can fingerprint the internal service inventory without any network-level access.

After the fix, all four ports collapse to the single `502 JdbcConnectFailed` envelope and the loop returns `429 Tellus:Connectivity:EgressRateLimited` after the 6-per-minute budget is spent.

remediation_steps: 1. Apply the rate limit to every caller. In `testRateLimit`, invert the exemption so the token bucket applies by default and only an explicit operator opt-out disables it (treat the env var as an opt-out `=== "0"` rather than an opt-in `!== "1"`). 2. ## Summary
`POST /api/v1/connectivity/connections/test-config` leaked an internal service fingerprint through two independent weaknesses that compounded:

1. The probe returned a **distinct HTTP error envelope per connect outcome** (closed port, open non-PG, PG auth failure, timeout), letting a caller map internal services by port and protocol family.
2. `testRateLimit` **exempted every authenticated principal** from the request rate limit, so the sweep was unthrottled.

This change closes both.

## Changes
- `testRateLimit`: the authenticated bypass is now an explicit operator **opt-out** (`CONNECTIVITY_TEST_RATE_LIMIT_ALL === "0"`); by default the 6-per-minute token bucket applies to authenticated callers too.
- `testConfig` error mapping: the auth-failure branch now returns the same `502 Tellus:Connectivity:JdbcConnectFailed` envelope as connect failures and timeouts, so the HTTP response no longer discloses whether a socket to the target succeeded or what kind of service answered. The fine-grained classification is preserved server-side in `observeProbe` metrics and the `console.warn` log.

## Verification
- Re-probed the same port set post-change: all outcomes collapse to the single `502 JdbcConnectFailed` envelope, and repeated probes exhaust the bucket and return `429 Tellus:Connectivity:EgressRateLimited`.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` passes.

## Note on scope
The reserved-target egress blocker (`assertEgressForConfig` / `assertEgressResolved`) is unchanged and continues to refuse non-allowlisted internal targets; this fix targets the **response-side oracle on allowed targets** and the missing velocity cap.

title: RCE: un-gated legacy ontology Function register+invoke escapes Node vm sandbox to host command execution
description: Any low-priv authenticated user (e.g. a **viewer**) can register an arbitrary TypeScript **Function** through the legacy ontology route and immediately invoke it, escaping the Node `vm` sandbox to execute arbitrary OS commands on the host as the API process user. The route carries **no** `authorizePublish()` gate, no transpile/import validation, and no audit — the publish-authorization boundary documented for the Functions executor is wired only to the canonical `/api/v1/functions/:rid/versions` and `/api/v1/code-repositories/:rid/tags` endpoints, not to this parallel legacy router.
impact: A viewer-level principal achieves **remote code execution on the host running the API**: the PoC returned `uid=501(olivierhabimana) gid=20(staff)` and hostname `Olivier-HABIMANA.local` from `child_process.execSync` executed inside the "sandboxed" function, and `fs.writeFileSync` wrote/read a file on the host. The compromised process environment exposes database credentials — the sandbox read `PGPASSWORD` and `POSTGRES_URL` (plus `PGUSER`/`PGDATABASE`/`PGHOST`) — enabling full compromise of the ontology database and lateral movement. Any tenant user with valid credentials can take over the API host identity.
technical_analysis:
Two layered failures combine into a complete low-priv → host RCE chain.

**1. Authorization gap (publish gate bypass).** `src/server.ts:1293` mounts the legacy router at `/api/v1/ontology/:ontologyId/functions`. Within it, `src/routes/functions.ts` handler `POST /` (line 28) inserts a new row into `ontology_function` and `ontology_function_version` directly from the request's raw `sourceCode`, and `POST /:apiName/invoke` (line 160) executes it. **Neither handler calls `authorizePublish()`** — the documented "only explicitly authorized authors may publish executable Functions" stopgap (`src/services/functions/executionPolicy.ts`) is enforced only on the newer TypeScript-Functions endpoints. So the entire publish trust boundary is trivially sidestepped via this parallel route; a mere authenticated principal is sufficient.

**2. Sandbox escape (vm is not a boundary).** Execution uses `runSandboxed(source_code, input)` (`src/routes/functions.ts:196`), which runs the source with Node's `vm` module **in the main API process event loop** (`src/services/functionRuntime.ts`, `vm.createContext(context)` at line 61/109 and `new vm.Script(...).runInContext(...)` at line 62/112). A `vm` context shares the host heap, and the global-proxy `this` retains a reachable `constructor.constructor` chain to the host `Function` constructor. `this.constructor.constructor("return process")()` therefore returns the **real host `process` object**, from which `process.mainModule.require("child_process")` (or `process.constructor("return require")()`) yields `child_process`/`fs`/`http`. The claimed mitigations in the file header (no `require`, no `process`, no `fs`) apply only to *non-escaped* code and do not survive this well-known escape class; unlike the production path there is not even a worker-thread separation or env whitelist here.

title: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via code-repositories working-tree function invoke (vm sandbox escape to host command execution)
description: The working-tree function invoke endpoint `POST /api/v1/code-repositories/:rid/functions/invoke` accepts raw TypeScript `inlineSource` and executes it server-side while requiring **no credentials at all**. Because authentication is not enforced for this route in the running configuration and the code runs in a Node `vm` that is trivially escaped, any remote unauthenticated attacker achieves arbitrary OS command execution as the host user running the API (validated: `uid=501(olivierhabimana)` on the developer's macOS host).
impact: Full remote code execution on the host running the tellus API without any authentication. The PoC executes `id && hostname && sw_vers` on the target and returns the output of the live host (macOS 26.3.1, user `olivierhabimana`). An attacker can read/write files, exfiltrate the database via the app's own PG credentials, pivot into the network, or destroy the environment.
technical_analysis:
**1. Unauthenticated admission.** The route `POST /api/v1/code-repositories/:rid/functions/invoke` is mounted under the `/api/v1/code-repositories` prefix, which `src/middleware/globalAuth.ts` (line ~195) allowlists globally. Its own guard `requireCodeReposAuth` (src/services/codeRepos/middleware/principal.ts) substitutes a dev "fallback principal" when `CODE_REPOS_TEST_AUTH=1` and `NODE_ENV != production`. **2. No publish/authorization gate.** The handler accepts `inlineSource` (raw source, "edit-and-run without commit") and executes it immediately. The `authorizePublish()` boundary in `executionPolicy.ts` is only wired into the *registry publish* endpoints, not this working-tree invoke. So arbitrary code runs with no publish authorization whatsoever.

**3. Node `vm` sandbox escape.** Execution flows through the worker-pool / `runSandboxed` path built on Node's `vm` module, which shares the host heap. The classic constructor-chain escape `globalThis.constructor.constructor("return process")()` returns the real host `process`; from there `require("child_process")` yields arbitrary command execution. The documented mitigations (require shim, env whitelist, no process/fs) do not stop this escape.

See the sibling report for the companion registry-publish primitive; this report covers the invoke + escape chain reachable without any credentials.

title: Remote Code Execution via Transforms preview/test executes arbitrary Python as the backend user (no publish trust gate, insecure local execution default)
description: The Tellus transforms pipeline executes user-controlled Python through `POST /api/v1/code-repositories/:rid/transforms/preview` and `POST /api/v1/code-repositories/:rid/transforms/test`. Unlike the Functions publish path, these endpoints are gated only by the Compass `WRITE` (EDITOR/OWNER) check — there is **no** `authorizePublish()` trust gate — and the executor defaults to **local host Python with no container/OS isolation**. Any principal able to write a code repository (and, in the current dev configuration, even a low-privilege viewer via the localhost dev-fallback principal) can therefore run arbitrary operating-system commands as the backend(Node.js) user and read/write the host filesystem.
impact: Full arbitrary code execution in the context of the backend Node process. Demonstrated live: `id` returns `uid=501(olivierhabimana) gid=20(staff)…`; `whoami` returns `olivierhabimana`; `hostname` returns `Olivier-HABIMANA.local`; `/etc/passwd` is read; an arbitrary file `/tmp/tellus_transform_pwn.txt` is written to the host filesystem. The attacker inherits all of the Node user's filesystem permissions and can pivot to adjacent services, persistence, and lateral movement. (In the current default the code runs in an unsandboxed local child process, not a container.) The spawned child's environment is correctly scrubbed of DB credentials by `filterEnv()`, so primary DB env credentials are not directly leaked — but the code executes with the full authority of the API user and its filesystem access.
technical_analysis:
**Gating asymmetry (root cause).** Tellus treats a published TypeScript Function as high-trust: publication requires `authorizePublish()` (`src/services/functions/executionPolicy.ts`) — a Keycloak `function:publish` role, an active `function_publish_grants` DB row, the legacy env allowlist, or open-development mode — and every decision is audit-logged, because the Function executor (`worker_threads` + `vm`) is explicitly documented as **not** a security boundary. The transform pipeline executes the same trust class of attacker code (arbitrary Python driving PySpark / host OS) but is protected only by `requireOperation({ operation: "WRITE" })` (`src/services/codeRepository/transforms/routes.ts`), whose `DEFAULT_POLICY` (`src/services/codeRepos/middleware/compass.ts:70`) allows WRITE whenever `principal.roles` contains `OWNER` or `EDITOR`. No `authorizePublish()`, no `function:publish` role, no `function_publish_grants` check exists anywhere on the transform path.

**Insecure default execution.** `executionMode()` (`src/services/codeRepository/transforms/executor.ts:43`) returns `"local"` unless `TELLUS_TRANSFORM_EXECUTION_MODE=container` is set. In local mode `runChild()` (executor.ts:498) `spawn(resolveTransformPython(), [driverPath], { cwd: workdir, env: filterEnv()+TELLUS_TRANSFORM_JOB })` — an ordinary host child process with no `--network=none`, no `--read-only`, no resource caps other than a timeout, and no user namespace.

**No-commit arbitrary code.** `runTransformPreview` (`src/services/codeRepository/transforms/previewHarness.ts:176-183`) merges request-supplied `fileOverrides` over the committed tree and passes the merged sources to `executeTransform` (previewHarness.ts:241), so even the repo-commit step is optional; an `entryPoint` + `fileOverrides` containing a `@transform_pandas(output=Output(...))` is discovered and its `compute()` body invoked.

The Python driver (`driver.py`) emits its result JSON as the **last** stdout line; any attacker `print()` precedes it and is returned verbatim in the preview response `stdout`, giving a clean read-back channel for recon output even though the executor subsequently reports "transform produced no parseable result".

1. Apply the publish trust gate to transform execution. Thread the resulting decision (and fail-closed on error) into `runTransformPreview`/`runTransformDryRun`/`startBuild`.

fix_pr_body:
Mitigate arbitrary code execution through the transforms pipeline.

Transforms execute user-supplied Python in the backend context, but today the only control is a per-repo Compass `WRITE` (EDITOR/OWNER) check, and execution defaults to an **un-isolated local child process** unless `TELLUS_TRANSFORM_EXECUTION_MODE=container` is set. The Functions pipeline (equivalent trust class) already requires `authorizePublish()`; transforms require nothing comparable. `runTransformPreview` also accepts `fileOverrides`, so arbitrary code can be executed without even committing to the repository.

Changes:
- Add an `authorizePublish()`-backed trust gate applied to `POST /:rid/transforms/test`, `POST /:rid/transforms/preview`, and the build/retry endpoints in `src/services/codeRepository/transforms/routes.ts`.
- Make `executionMode()` in `src/services/codeRepository/transforms/executor.ts` default to `"container"` and only allow `"local"` behind an explicit `TELLUS_TRANSFORM_ALLOW_LOCAL=1` + non-production `NODE_ENV`, failing closed otherwise.
- Require the trust decision before `executeTransform()` whenever `fileOverrides` is supplied (defense-in-depth against no-commit execution).
